pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, repeated reasoning turns into deriving and rule-describing: using a known double to get a near-double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 always drops the tens digit by one, and stating a rule for a sequence ('add 5 each time, so the ones digit alternates 0, 5'). The MP8 habit is to notice the repeated step, articulate it as a rule, and use it to predict — while checking it actually holds. Teaching should make the known fact and the derived one adjacent (a double and its near-double side by side) and press for the rule in the child's words, then test it on a fresh case.
bestPractices: Put a doubles fact next to its near-double (6+6 and 6+7) so the '+1' adjustment is seen, not computed from scratch
Ask the child to state the rule ('what's happening each time?') and then test it on the next case to guard against a rule taken from too few examples
Use a hundred square / place-value cards so −10 visibly drops the tens digit each time
Record a sequence and its step so the repeating structure and its rule are both on show ('+5, +5, +5')
keyRepresentations: Doubles and near-doubles on ten-frames / cubes (double + 1)
Hundred square and place-value cards for ±10
Number line marked with equal repeated steps (+5)
Bead strings for repeated addition patterns
commonMisconceptions: Recomputes 6+7 from one, not seeing it as the known double 6+6 plus 1
Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly (adds 2, or doubles the larger number)
States a rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing
Subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones instead of dropping the tens digit

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, this topic builds the habit of looking for and expressing regularity in repeated reasoning (MP8): deriving a near-double from a known double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 from a two-digit number drops the tens digit by one, and stating a sequence rule ('+5 each time starting from 5, so the ones digit alternates 5, 0') — then TESTING that rule on a fresh case rather than trusting it from one or two examples. Core teaching moves: place a known fact adjacent to the derived one so the adjustment is seen not recomputed, press for the rule in the child's own words, and always test the generalisation on a new case.

activities.title: Near-doubles builder: the double plus one
feedback: If the child counts up from 6 (or from 1) rather than referring to 6+6, put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side so the single extra cube is visible, and name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'.
If the child says 6+7=14 (added two) or doubles the 7, use the two rows to show exactly ONE cube was added — steady the adjustment; no need to reteach doubles.
Probe flexibility: 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 instead (one less than 14)? which double is handiest here?'
activities.rationale: Making the known fact and the derived one physically adjacent lets the '+1' be observed rather than computed, which is the derive-from-known-facts habit the guidance describes and keeps the derivation visible before fading support; repeating the adjustment across 6+7, 6+8 and 7+8 begins the repeated-reasoning shortcut.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
learnerActions: Set out two rows of 6 cubes (or two ten-frames of 6) and confirm the double: 6+6=12.
Add exactly ONE more cube to one row and say the new total: 6+7=13. State it as 'the double I know, and one more'.
Repeat for 6+8 ('two more than the double, so 14') and for another double you know, e.g. 7+7=14 so 7+8=15.
Say aloud which double you used and how many you adjusted by, before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: A near-double can be derived from an adjacent known double by adjusting, instead of counting up from one.

activities.title: State a rule, then test it
feedback: If the child announces 'it's add 5' after two terms and won't check, do not simply confirm or correct it — ask 'how could we be sure? test the next one' so the checking habit forms.
If a later term surprises the child, treat the surprise as the lesson: a rule from too few cases can be wrong; revise and re-test.
Ask 'your rule is add 5 — what will the ones digit of the next three terms be? how do you know?' to check the rule predicts, not just describes.
activities.rationale: Recording the sequence and its step together — on a number line or bead string as well as in writing — puts the repeating structure and its rule both on show (representations making the structure visible), and requiring a test on the next case guards against a generalisation drawn from too few examples.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: Lay out the first few terms of a sequence (e.g. 5, 10, 15, 20) and say the repeating step out loud: '+5, +5, +5'. Optionally show the equal +5 jumps on a number line or bead string so the repeating structure is visible.
State the rule in your own words: 'each time we add 5'. Predict the NEXT term before extending.
Predict the ones digit of the next three terms (25, 30, 35) and say why ('they alternate 5, 0, 5').

TEST it: have the adult reveal the next term of the given sequence (e.g. uncover a hidden card or the next group on the bead string) and compare it with your prediction; if it does not match, revise the rule. Extending the sequence yourself with your own rule is not a test.
Then say how you could be sure a rule is right before trusting it.
activities.intendedInsight: A rule guessed from a couple of cases should be tested on fresh cases before we rely on it: a passing test makes us more confident (it does not prove the rule), while one failing case shows the rule needs revising — this is the MP8 discipline of checking a generalisation.

activities.title: Subtracting 10 on a hundred square — and bounding the rule
feedback: If the child subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones, use the hundred square to show the move is one whole row back (straight up on a square with 1 in the top row; straight down on a square numbered from the bottom) — the ones digit does not change.
Counterexample to bound the rule: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does take away ONE do that to 45?' (45−1=44) to check the child limits the rule to −10.
Confirm by reading the place-value cards: the tens card goes down one, the ones card is untouched.
activities.rationale: A hundred square or place-value cards make the −10 move structural rather than counted, and testing whether −1 behaves the same teaches the child to bound a generalisation to its conditions and evaluate reasonableness.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: On a hundred square (or with place-value cards), start at a two-digit number such as 45 and subtract 10; land on 35 and notice the tens digit dropped by one while the ones digit stayed the same.
Repeat from two or three other starting numbers to see the same pattern each time; state the rule: 'take away 10 drops the tens digit by one'.
Test the boundary: does taking away ONE do the same thing? Try 45−1 (which gives 44) and see it does not — so the rule is only for −10.
Say the rule in your own words AND what it does NOT cover.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting 10 from a two-digit number lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — and a good rule is stated with the conditions under which it holds.

activities.title: Check-in: which fact did you use?
feedback: A correct number alone does not show repeated-reasoning insight — follow up with 'which fact did you use?' because a scored blank does not reveal whether the rule was reasoned or guessed.
If the child recomputes from one, redirect to the adjacent known double before accepting the answer.
activities.rationale: Fill-in and sequence-continuation items can confirm a correct answer, but because scoring alone cannot reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned or guessed, pair every item with a 'how did you get it?' question. This is a check, best used after hands-on work; it verifies recall and continuation without by itself eliciting the child's reasoning.
learnerActions: Answer short derivation prompts such as '6+6=12, so 6+7=__' and 'continue the sequence 5, 10, 15, __'.
For each answer, say WHICH known fact or rule you used to get it, not just the number.
Try at least one where you explain how you'd check your answer is reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: Getting the right number is not enough; the target is reusing a known fact or rule and being able to justify it.

constraints: This is a META/mathematical-thinking topic for ages 6-7: the goal is the derive-and-check habit, not just correct totals. Listen for reuse of a known fact and the adjustment, not just the answer 13.

Fill-in or sequence-continuation checks can show whether a correct answer was produced but cannot by themselves reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned, recalled or guessed; always pair with 'which fact did you use?' and treat them as a follow-up to hands-on building, not a replacement.

A static near-doubles card or annotated −10 column can illustrate the move for reference, but does not let the child adjust the quantity or test a self-stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Bound the −10 rule explicitly: it lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — this specific 'drop the tens by one' rule does not generalise to −1 or other amounts.
Do not confirm or correct a child's sequence rule for them when the aim is building the checking habit; prompt them to test the next case instead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original recommendation leaned on a specific interactive 'near-doubles builder' and 'sequence machine' and rated conversation and 3D artefacts 'poor'. Those comparative/necessity ratings are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the concrete affordances (live total update when a cube is added, a machine flagging a wrong predicted term) are preserved here as optional ways to make the mechanism visible, achievable with physical cubes, ten-frames, number lines, bead strings, hundred squares, or screen tools.

The original claims that '3D adds no structural information' and that 'open dialogue gives nothing concrete' were omitted as unsupported universal statements; spoken explanation of which fact was used is in fact central to assessing this reasoning habit, while a sort or fill-in check alone verifies classification/recall without eliciting that explanation.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 6+6=12, 6+7=13, 6+8=14, 7+7=14, 7+8=15, 45−10=35, 45−1=44 all check out; the sequence 5,10,15,20 continuing 25,30,35 has ones digits alternating 5,0,5. Independent re-review found no arithmetic or logic errors to correct.
The number-line (+5) and bead-string representations from the original keyRepresentations are retained as optional supports in the sequence activity.

Independent re-review adjusted only source attribution: the EEF visible-representation claim was added to Activity 2 because its rationale directly invokes representations making the repeating structure visible. No learner-facing error was found.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 to get 6+7 as well? which double is handiest?' to test flexible reuse of known facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does taking away ten from 45 give 35? what about taking away ONE?' to check the child bounds the rule to −10
Ask 'your rule is add 5 — what will the ones digit of the next three terms be? how do you know?' to probe whether the rule predicts, not just describes
Ask 'how could you check your rule is right before trusting it?' to surface the MP8 habit of testing a generalisation
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving from the known double: '6+7 is one more than 6+6, so 13; 6+8 is two more, so 14.' The reuse of the known fact and the adjustment, not just 13, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Recomputes 6+7 from one instead of seeing it as the known double 6+6 plus 1
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side on ten-frames so the single extra cube is visible; name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts up from 6 (or from 1) rather than referring to 6+6

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly — adds two, or doubles the 7 instead of the 6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with the two ten-frames to see exactly ONE cube was added; do not reteach doubles, just steady the adjustment

errorPatterns.pattern: States a sequence rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing further
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT simply confirm or correct the rule; ask 'how could we be sure? test the next one' so the habit of checking a generalisation forms
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces 'it's add 5' after two terms and won't check, or is surprised when a later term breaks their rule

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes each sum from one, mis-adjusts near-doubles, and states rules without testing; each result treated as new
responseLevels.full: Independently derives from known facts (double ± 1, −10 drops the tens digit), states a sequence rule AND tests it on a fresh case, and predicts confidently — transferring the derive-and-check habit unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives a near-double or continues a sequence when prompted, but does not reuse known facts independently or check that a stated rule holds

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know 6 + 6 = 12. Use that to work out 6 + 7 quickly, without counting from one. Then tell me how it would help with 6 + 8.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching 13 by counting up shows no repeated-reasoning insight; deriving it as 'the double plus one' does. A child using the structure adjusts the known fact and extends the idea to 6+8; a child without it recounts each sum from the start.
